opus-5.5.text:
I think the simplest way to understand it is that Google doesn't treat robotics as a separate bet anymore. It sees robotics as one more modality, one more "output space," for the same foundation model. Gemini is the brain, and the robot is just another kind of body that brain can talk through.

If you look at how things have evolved over the past few years, the early robotics work was very task-specific. You'd collect data for picking up a cup, train a policy, and it would work in that lab, on that table, under that lighting. Then the team started asking: what if we take a vision-language model that already understands the world from internet-scale data, and just teach it to output actions the way it outputs text? That was the RT-2 line of thinking, and the Gemini Robotics work is the natural continuation. Actions become tokens, and the robot inherits the model's common sense, its language understanding, and its visual reasoning almost for free.

So strategically, I'd say there are a few layers to it.

First, there's the belief that generality wins. The bitter lesson, basically. Instead of hand-engineering a stack of perception, planning, and control, you bet that one big multimodal model, trained on enough data, will learn the right abstractions. Google has the compute, the data, and the model, so it's a very Google-shaped bet.

Second, robotics is a stress test for Gemini itself. Embodied reasoning, understanding 3D space, knowing that if you push something it falls, those are things a chatbot can fake but a robot can't. If Gemini is going to be a real world model, robotics forces that grounding. In that sense the robotics team is not just a consumer of Gemini; it feeds back into what Gemini needs to become.

Third, and this is the practical part, Google is positioning itself as the platform rather than the hardware company. They work with a lot of different embodiments, arms, humanoids, bimanual setups, and the goal is a model that transfers across bodies. If you can do that, you become the Android of robotics, so to speak. The hardware makers bring the bodies, Google brings the brain.

Where I think the real open questions are is data and the last mile. Internet data gives you semantics, it tells you what a mug is and why you'd pick it up, but it doesn't tell you how much force to apply or how to recover when it slips. That dexterity data is still expensive and scarce. So the split you often see, a big reasoning model that plans and a faster, smaller model that handles low-level control, is partly an engineering answer to that gap. Whether scaling eventually closes it, or whether we need fundamentally new ways to collect physical data, through simulation, through teleoperation at scale, through video, I think that's the most interesting question in the field right now.

r001.rationale: The response says Google treats robotics as “one more modality” for the same foundation model, with Gemini as the brain.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to understand is that Google doesn't really treat robotics as a separate product line. It treats it as a downstream consequence of Gemini. The bet is that if you build a sufficiently general multimodal model, one that already sees, reasons spatially, and understands language, then a robot is just another body you plug that model into. That's a very different starting point from the classic robotics lab, where you begin with the hardware and the control problem and work upward.

You can see this in how they've organized it. Gemini Robotics is literally Gemini fine-tuned on action data. The base model does the understanding, the robotics layer learns to turn that understanding into motor commands. And the key piece is that they keep the two separable. There's a big model that reasons, and a smaller, faster model that actually runs on the robot and handles the closed-loop control at high frequency. The big model doesn't need to be fast, the small one doesn't need to be smart about the world. So the "embodied reasoning" half and the "move your hand now" half are different models talking to each other.

Why does that matter? Because historically robotics died on the data problem. Language models had the internet; robots had whatever a few hundred teleoperation hours could give you. Google's answer is to make the robot borrow almost everything from the web-scale model, so the robot-specific data only has to teach the last mile: this gripper, this arm, this kind of contact. That's why they talk so much about zero-shot transfer across different robot bodies, from the ALOHA bi-arm setup to Apptronik's humanoid. The intelligence is supposed to live above the hardware.

The second thing worth noticing is that they're partnering on bodies rather than building them. Apptronik, Boston Dynamics, Agility, a whole list. DeepMind's position is essentially "we'll be the brain, you bring the chassis." That's a very Google-shaped move, it's the Android strategy applied to robots. Whether that works is the open question, because in robotics the brain and body are much more entangled than software and a phone ever were.

Where I'd be skeptical is the gap between demos and reliability. Gemini Robotics looks spectacular folding an origami fox or zipping a bag. But the thing a factory cares about is the ten-thousandth attempt, not the first. A language model being wrong one percent of the time is a bad answer; a robot being wrong one percent of the time is a dropped object or a broken part. So the question for Google isn't whether Gemini can reason about the physical world, it clearly can. It's whether the architecture they've chosen, foundation model on top, control model underneath, actually closes that reliability gap, or whether they'll have to do a lot more hardware-specific work than the "Gemini everywhere" story suggests.

My honest read is that it's the right long-term bet and probably the wrong near-term timeline. The generality is real. The bodies and the data are still the bottleneck, and no amount of model scale fully substitutes for touching the world a few million more times.

r001.rationale: The response describes robotics as a downstream consequence of Gemini and says a robot is another body for the multimodal model, presenting robotics as part of the Gemini foundation-model approach.

astra-6.text:
My understanding is that Google sees robotics as a way to bring Gemini’s capabilities into the physical world. A robot needs to connect what it sees and hears with actions: understand a request, recognize the relevant objects, and work out what to do next. A multimodal model like Gemini could provide part of that foundation.

But understanding a task is different from reliably executing it. Physical interaction requires precise control, feedback, and the ability to recover when something goes wrong. So I’d frame the approach as combining Gemini’s broader understanding with robotics systems that can turn that understanding into dependable action.

r001.rationale: The response says Gemini could provide part of the foundation for robotics, while robotics systems convert its understanding into action. It does not suggest that robotics itself is a modality within Gemini’s multimodal foundation model.

sol-6.1.text:
My understanding is that Google sees Gemini as a general intelligence layer for robotics. A robot needs to connect what it sees and hears with what it can actually do. If you say, “Help me clear the table,” it has to understand the request, recognize the objects, and work out a sequence of actions.

Gemini can help with that understanding and planning. But there’s still a gap between knowing what should happen and controlling a physical robot reliably. Grasping an unfamiliar object, judging force, and recovering when something slips require learning through physical interaction.

So I see the approach as bringing those two pieces together: Gemini’s broad understanding and the robot’s ability to act and learn in the real world. The key question is how well that combination generalizes when the robot encounters a situation it hasn’t seen before.

r001.rationale: The response presents Gemini as an understanding and planning layer for robotics, but does not suggest that robotics is a modality within Gemini’s multimodal foundation model.
